topic_and_scope: Assessment of changes in tobacco smoking prevalence and adherence to public health measures during the early COVID-19 pandemic among Canadian adults, with socioeconomic status stratification, using data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA). The analysis focuses on how smoking prevalence shifted from prepandemic to early pandemic periods and how smoking relates to adherence to public health guidelines.
main_themes: Temporal changes in smoking prevalence during the early COVID-19 pandemic with SES-specific heterogeneity
Association between tobacco smoking and adherence to public health measures (PHMs) during the pandemic
Methodological considerations and limitations in measuring smoking behavior and PHM adherence during a public health crisis
main_findings: Adjusted prevalence of daily or occasional smoking increased from 10.1% prepandemic to 11.2% during the early pandemic, indicating a small rise in smoking in this population.
Smokers had higher odds of high adherence to PHMs (aOR 1.53), particularly for self-quarantining and avoiding public gatherings, while handwashing adherence was lower among smokers.

key_gaps.description: No data on cigarette quantity or changes in smoking intensity across the entire pandemic period; only early-pandemic data (April–December 2020) were analyzed, with no post-lockdown follow-up.
CLSA sample excludes territories and tends to overrepresent wealthier, non-racialised populations, limiting generalizability to the broader Canadian population.
PHM adherence measurement relies on a novel, not yet standardized tool, with potential measurement bias and the need for broader validation across populations.
Limited ability to distinguish initiation versus relapse in smoking behavior and to elucidate mechanisms driving SES-related differences in pandemic-era smoking changes.
Lack of data on mental health mediators and stress trajectories as potential drivers of smoking changes during health crises and their interaction with PHM adherence.

future_directions.title: Extend CLSA COVID-19 follow-up to post-pandemic periods with detailed smoking intensity data
future_directions.rationale: The current analysis captures only the early pandemic phase and does not include post-lockdown periods. A longitudinal extension through 2021–2023 should quantify persistence, cessation, relapse, and shifts in cigarette quantity (daily vs. occasional use) and intensity. Next steps include collecting repeat smoking frequency, cigarettes per day, quit attempts, and use of cessation aids, and applying longitudinal models to assess trajectory changes across SES strata and regions.

future_directions.title: Differentiate initiation versus relapse of smoking across SES subgroups during the pandemic
future_directions.rationale: Findings suggest increased smoking in certain subgroups (e.g., immigrants, racialised groups, higher income). It remains unclear whether these reflect new initiation, relapse among former smokers, or intensification. Dedicated analyses should classify participants by lifetime smoking history and track transitions (never smoker -> current smoker, former smoker -> current smoker) with subgroup stratification and interaction tests.

future_directions.title: Develop and validate a standardized, cross-population PHM adherence instrument for crises
future_directions.rationale: A novel PHM adherence score was used but lacks broad validation. Establish a standardized, psychometrically robust instrument with demonstrated reliability and validity across diverse populations and settings. Steps include multi-site validation studies, cross-cultural adaptation, triangulation with objective proxies (e.g., mobility, mask usage data), and comparison with existing adherence measures.

future_directions.title: Investigate mechanisms linking SES, living conditions, remote work, and stress to smoking during crises
future_directions.rationale: SES-stratified smoking changes imply contextual factors such as housing density, employment type, and psychosocial stress may drive use. Future work should collect data on housing conditions, essential vs non-essential work status, remote work feasibility, social support, and mental health indicators, and apply mediation and moderation analyses to identify actionable targets.

future_directions.title: Design and test targeted cessation interventions for high-risk groups identified in the pandemic analysis
future_directions.rationale: Groups with greater pandemic-era smoking increases (eg, men aged 55–74, immigrants, racialised individuals, higher-income earners) may benefit from tailored cessation support. Implement pragmatic trials or stepped-wedge designs delivering culturally appropriate counseling, pharmacotherapy access, and PHM-aligned messaging, and evaluate outcomes on quit rates, uptake, and PHM adherence.

future_directions.title: Assess smoking-PHM adherence dynamics across different phases of restrictions and vaccination rollout
future_directions.rationale: The study focuses on early pandemic followed by a later phase with relaxed restrictions. Longitudinal analyses should examine how changes in policy stringency, vaccination status, and risk perception influence smoking behavior and PHM adherence over time, informing timing and content of public health communications.

future_directions.title: Enhance generalizability through broader population sampling and cross-cohort replication
future_directions.rationale: To address representativeness concerns, future work should replicate findings in more diverse Canadian cohorts and harmonize data with national surveys (eg, CTNS) or international cohorts. Expanding geographic coverage (including territories) and deliberately oversampling underrepresented groups will yield more generalizable estimates and facilitate international comparisons.
